entry.title: Reasoning through natural language and latents

link.title: Reasoning through natural language and latents

entry.content:
Generating domain-specific data using natural language

A key question on many people’s minds is how to leverage recent advances in both large language models (LLMs) and domain-specific generative models. Fortunately, LLM-to-Flow Distillation (LFD) proposes a succinct solution: (1) ask an LLM how to solve your specific problem using a generative model for your scientific domain, (2) use the generative model to design some new data, (3) assess that new data with the LLM and create subgoals for the generative model to reach, (4) use direct preference optimization (DPO) to steer the generative model’s latent representations into a promising direction (according to the LLM’s feedback), and (5) rinse and repeat until goal convergence.

This is, of course, a simplification of the process, but at a high level, LFD modifies domain-specific generative models to produce data increasingly in alignment with the user’s specified goal through iterative subgoals and DPO. Since this blueprint is domain-agnostic, one can imagine how it will be applied across scientific disciplines in the coming years. If this work piques your interest, its source code can be found on GitHub.

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Reasoning with biomolecular latents

The Baker Lab at the University of Washington recently released their latest version of the popular protein design model RFdiffusion, titled RFD4-Proteina (as a collaborative nod to the Proteina family of protein models from NVIDIA). In contrast to previous editions of RFdiffusion, RFD4-Proteina features all-atom latent space generative modeling for protein design tasks. Similar to Zatom-2, its architecture features physics-based supervision to improve the fidelity of its generated samples.

Most notably, RFD4-Proteina supports a large number of protein binder design tasks that have been validated by wet-lab experiments, e.g., targeting nucleic acids, ligands, complexes, and more. Such promising experimental results suggest that RFD4-Proteina’s new intrinsic and extrinsic reasoning capabilities, alongside its diversely pretrained generative latent space, have endowed it with rich biomolecular design prowess compared to existing protein design models. As usual for the Baker Lab, its source code can generously be found on GitHub.

Reflections

How do you think the interplay between ambient space generative modeling and latent space generative models will play out? Are there fundamental capabilities that latent space generators can achieve which ambient space models cannot? And how will domain-specific generators like RFD4-Proteina best be paired with large language models for scientific discovery? Using the LFD template, or via some other means?

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

entry.title: Roughly we go into that good night

link.title: Roughly we go into that good night

entry.content:
Books Read in October 2026

  1. Subliminal
  2. My Inventions: The Autobiography of Nikola Tesla
  3. The Elements of Marie Curie
  4. The Singularlity is Nearer
  5. Speaker for the Dead

Unconscious and unseen

How can old memories and nearly imperceptible phenomena sway what decisions we make? Answer: the unconscious says so. Subliminal captures the feeling of wonder that arises upon discovering how peculiar the human mind’s inner workings truly are. Notably, the book is comprised of many first and third-hand accounts of contexts where one’s mental intuitions have been automatically bypassed in favor of deep-seated cognitive templates our minds have developed over the years. As such, this work has implications for several aspects of our lives, including our relationships, vocations, and community structures.

The Whiz Kid

Tesla, oh Tesla…Nikola Tesla, that is. What an eccentric fellow, who went on to develop transformative technologies, such as the Tesla coil and the transformer (n.b., not the AI one). His autobiography poignantly presents Tesla’s inner monologue as he grows and matures as both a human being and an inventor. There are many lessons we can learn from a life like Tesla’s, such as the time and attention often required to become true creatives within a given industry. One part intuition, many parts perspiration.

Time will tell a story

Marie Curie is one of the most recognizable names in science. Not only did she win two Nobel Prizes, but she was also the first non-male to win any. Her work on radioactivity, among many other endeavors, quickly launched Marie and her husband/collaborator Pierre into the scientific limelight. As documented in The Elements of Marie Curie, what stands out most to me about Marie is how dedicated she was to scientific mentorship alongside research. As several women scientists were eager to start their own research labs, Marie provided the training grounds necessary for them to launch their careers, acting as a force multiplier for heterogeneous scientific talent pools.

Woh, that fast?

Long ago, I heard of a book called The Singularity is Near. When I went to read it, little did I know at the time that the author, Ray Kurzweil, published its sequel under the similar title The Singularity is Nearer. So I accidentally read the sequel rather than the original, but in hindsight, I think this worked out well. Since machine learning has advanced exponentially over the last 15 years, an updated synposis of Kurzweil’s views on AI, digital twins, and digital biology was long overdue. Having finished the book, I can confidentally say that it will challenge most readers to consider how quickly the world will change in the next decade, in particular how our self-conceptions will rapidly evolve with AI.

Jesus and Hitler, two for the price of one

The sequel to Ender’s Game, Speaker for the Dead, does not disappoint. In fact, its philosophical undertones came across rather naturally as the story wrestles with describing its protagonist as both savior of humanity and a genocidal mastermind (n.b., you were right, Kyle!). How would you view yourself if you were tricked into committing an alien genocide but later lauded by your species as a hero? Speaker for the Dead explores these themes with delicate precision, building on the worlds and characters of its well-known prequel.

Alex

entry.title: Climbing science’s many scales
entry.content:
Learn physics to decode chemistry and biology

Recent trends in scientific machine learning have hinted that physics-grounded training objectives may represent atomistic machine learning’s closest analog to the expressiveness of image reconstruction in computer vision. In this spirit, with Zatom-2, researchers at the University of Cambridge and beyond have studied a new way of pretraining atomistic generative models (disclosure: conflict of interest).

Zatom-2’s key idea is to unify atomistic tasks and data with a single tokenization scheme, consisting of: (1) the new atom1 tokenizer for chemical (molecule and material) data, which infers (atom) element types and lattice geometry parameters from 3D coordinate representations alone; and (2) atom14 for biological (protein) data, which infers amino acid (token) sequences from such geometric representations as well. In this setting, multitask pretraining, in particular with energy and force prediction tasks, empirically provides the best generative modeling configuration for molecule and material data, and also yields the best transfer learning results for protein generation tasks. If you’re curious to learn more about this work, its source code, documentation, and model weights are freely available.

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Harder, better, faster, stronger

Multiple sequence alignments are a key idea in AI for biology these days, thanks primarily to AlphaFold. What is not as well understood is how such multi-sequence alignments might be useful for learning rich representations in other domains of science. In CellMSA, the authors propose to refactor such alignments into the context of single-cell biology, to learn cellular representations for downstream tasks.

With an AlphaFold-inspired, multi-sequence-equipped architecture in hand, CellMSA delivers strong performance across a range of cellular prediction tasks, suggesting that the pairwise gene representations learned from its cell-gene sequence alignments are broadly useful for cellular biology. For those interested in learning more, CellMSA’s source code is available on GitHub.

Reflections

How may physics inform the representations of generative models going forward? How might cellular representation learning benefit from enhanced physical (biological) supervision or transfer? In the future, do you think scaling laws might hold between low-level physical domains and higher-order biological domains?

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

entry.title: Reading into historical figures
entry.content:
Books Read in September 2026

  1. 1491
  2. The Nvidia Way
  3. The Autobiography of Benjamin Franklin
  4. Four Thousand Weeks
  5. Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track

It didn’t always look like this

1491, a sober account of life in North and South America before Columbus’ arrival, provides a corrective historical lens for how we should view the level of ecological and technological development common among indigeneous American societies of that era. Rather than “living lightly” on the land, indigeneous communities are known to have been intentional sculptors of their ecological environments, through techniques such as regular burnings, irrigation, and agriculture. Interestingly, indigeneous societies were arguably more advanced and well-populated than their European counterparts in this time period, providing examples of how separately developed civilizations can ultimately develop similar technologies and social structures without direct communication or exchange.

Racing for chips

What is there to say about Nvidia’s history other than “woh”! From early graphics chip manufacturing for accelerating computing workflows (e.g., video games, simulations) to deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and now digital biology - the breadth and depth of applications of graphics processing hardware is hard to understate. Growing up, I wouldn’t have predicted that the company that produced the graphics cards I liked to purchase for playing Steam PC games would become a pivotal element of the ongoing race to artificial general intelligence (AGI). Nonetheless, here we are, and to understand a bit of where the future may (further) lead, The Nvidia Way offers some insights from Nvidia’s past.

A founder in more than one way

Benjamin Franklin’s autobiography brings this historical figure to life in new ways for readers. First, its first-person perspective allows us to glimpse into the thought processes of one of the United States’ founding figures. In doing so, we begin to better grasp Franklin’s philosophy for how to live well within a community. Second, this autobiography presents glimmers of Franklin’s character, for example, how he thought about charity and the best ways to carry it out. The breadth of Franklin’s writings in this work are truly noteworthy, so I recommend it at the very least as an example of how one can conceptualize and reflect on one’s life through important seasons.

Accept your limitations and start saying no more

Is the following prompt relatable? “I have all the interests and I’ve said yes to nearly every related opportunity that’s come my way. Now, I have very little time for any one of these interests/priorities, so I feel like I’m making no progress on any specific task or direction. What do I do?” Four Thousand Weeks gives readers a useful exercise to try in these situations: reflect on your mortality, practice mindfulness to become more familiar with your feelings surrounding mortality, and then use the insights you gain by developing this familiarity to start saying no to many of these interests (at least for this season of life). Only by becoming keenly aware of how short and unpredictable life is can we begin to make wise decisions about how to spend our precious “four thousand weeks”.

Letters unto letters

How can one describe Richard Feynman in a few words? The answer: you can’t. Like all humans, he was too complicated to summarize into a simple caricature. However, Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track offers a touching viewpoint into Feynman’s life: his letters to and from friends, family, colleagues, and acquaintances. Through these letters, we see Feynman’s deep love for his wife, Arline, in their constant exchanges of life tidbits during her long-term fight with tuberculosis, as well as in Feynman’s poignant letter addressed to her after her passing. These letters also portray the complexities of Feynman’s character, that is, his flawed yet often altruistic motives as a scientist and educator.

Alex

entry.title: Navigating experiences and states
entry.content:
Books Read in August 2026

  1. Swann’s Way (In Search of Lost Time, #1)
  2. Sisters in Science
  3. The Infinity Machine
  4. Cryptonomicon

Surreal detail

“Proust can change your life” is a quote I’ve occassionally heard thrown around in tech circles. This got me curious to see what it is about Marcel Proust’s writings that resonates so deeply with certain readers. After finishing Swann’s Way, the first part of Proust’s expansive collection of essays In Search of Lost Time, I believe I understand part of the reason why: it’s his vivid descriptions of everyday life (thoughts, feelings, surroundings, experiences) that are like none other. Proust’s writing, albeit sometimes difficult to follow linearly, is ethereal in a keen sense, encouraging readers to lose track of time and immerse themselves in the world of his experiences.

Fleeing for safety, finding solidarity

During World War II, many women scientists in Germany quickly found their safety and employment situations uncertain. Sisters in Science documents their unique stories of how life in Germany soon became untenable for women scientists, particularly those of Jewish heritage. Out of desparate situations to secure work visas in the United States and elsewhere was born a tightnit community of women supporting one another in their journeys to restart their lives abroad. Importantly, in several cases, such women may never have met each other had the circumstances of their communication been different, illustrating the power of comradery amidst societal prejudice and persecution.

All eyes on AI

Not just another book about AI, The Infinity Machine introduces readers to one of its most influential and curious contemporary leaders: Demis Hassabis. Inspired by the prospect of “making sand think”, Demis began working on AI as a game developer in high school. From there, he continued exploring AI from different institutional angles, including academia and industry, until in 2010 he founded Google DeepMind, one of today’s frontier AI research labs producing AI models such as AlphaGo, MuZero, AlphaStar, AlphaFold, and Gemini. One of the unique contributions of this book is its dissection of Demis’ philosophy and why he believes AGI should be built (and how it will change our understanding of the universe as we know it).

Historical fiction, maybe?

Cryptonomicon is a whirlwind novel that jumps back and forth between the perspectives of World War II Allied-codebreakers and 1990s computer nerds who are motivated to spark social change through cryptography and information systems. Dazzling is the novel’s ability to balance both perspectives without overwhelming readers with detail. From the sandy beaches of the Philippines to the dreary TSA line in the San Francisco International Airport (SFO), this book keeps readers visualizing how both narratives will eventually interweave and converge into a compelling finale. For those curious to learn more about cryptography, Unix, World War II history, and how they all connect to modern day technologies, help yourselves.

Alex

entry.title: Unraveling intelligence across systems
entry.content:
Optimizing for novelty

Researchers at Tufts University have presented an alternative way of measuring epiplexity (i.e., learnable, structural information excluding random noise) to optimize algorithms for representational discovery. The key idea is to minimize the spectral description length of a (neural network) encoder’s feature representations, as a loss function in and of itself, which is surprisingly differentiable and modestly efficient using PyTorch operations such as torch.linalg.solve_triangular() and torch.linalg.svdvals().

This learnable novelty loss function can also be understood as maximizing the log-determinant of the regularized Fisher information matrix, whereby over time training is inducing “intelligence” by concentrating more Fisher information across representational dimensions that yield the most geometric volume per parameter. Imagine this process as maximizing the size of a Fisher ellipsoid in information space (thanks, @Mohamad Yassine, for this helpful analogy - https://www.alphaxiv.org/abs/2607.18433). Thankfully, the source code accompanying this learnable novelty paper can be found on GitHub.

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Enhancing representations for molecule generation

The idea of accelerating representation learning within generative models has received widespread attention in mainstream areas of machine learning (think REPA). However, this idea has recently begun surfacing in the realm of AI for science, in particular in molecular machine learning.

LENSEs is arguably one of the first compelling AI for science methods along this research direction. The idea is simple: take the embeddings of a pretrained molecular encoding model and teach a diffusion model to mimic these embeddings (and their respective inputs/outputs) while simultaneously denoising atomistic data. In doing so, one can jointly accelerate the diffusion model’s convergence speed and improve its sample quality. This idea will likely show up in other areas of AI for science in the near future.

Reflections

What do you think of representation alignment and learnable novelty and their role in scientific machine learning? Is their application straightforward in most computational settings, or will they require significant customization to achieve strong results in relevant research domains?

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

entry.title: A bittersweet lesson in the learning

link.title: A bittersweet lesson in the learning

entry.content:
Unearthing the foundations of continuous data

GenCeption from Google DeepMind recently proposed a new approach to building foundation models for visual data. The key idea is to take a pretrained diffusion generative model (for videos), freeze its autoencoder weights (if it’s a latent diffusion model), and finetune the diffusion model’s Diffusion Transformer (DiT) architecture for both dense and sparse visual representation tasks using learnable task and video tokens. Importantly, dense downstream tasks can reuse the model’s frozen decoder weights (if present), treating new representation learning/prediction tasks as a visual reconstruction objective.

This approach currently provides both high performance and wide coverage of tasks spanning computer vision, suggesting that, though a denoising objective, its pretrained DiT architecture has learned highly informative and broadly applicable representations of continuous (visual) data. This suggests that computer vision, perhaps alongside other (non-discrete) data domains, is beginning to identify the axes of neural scaling that are most effective beyond the next-token prediction paradigm prevalent in natural language processing. Scientific applications based on this idea are likely to follow suit. However, the nuances of what it takes to train such an informative generative model in different scientific domains will almost certainly require extra consideration.

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Discovering physical laws (through language)

Can large language models (LLMs) deduce the physical laws of novel simulated worlds through text-based interaction alone? If so, would this convince us that there is something inherently informative that LLMs are learning beyond distributions for next-token prediction? With the new DiscoverPhysics benchmark from Princeton, we can begin to (partially) address these questions.

DiscoverPhysics has a convenient leaderboard to track community progress on this task of uncovering novel physical laws, along with open-source code accompanying the benchmark. Interestingly, with the release of Anthropic’s Claude 5 Fable model, the leaderboard appears to have a new resolute leader in terms of per-world accuracy as well as explainability. Does this suggest that larger models are simply more likely to find better (and more interpretable) solutions to physical phenomena than smaller models (re: epiplexity)?

Reflections

What are the implications of neural scaling for different scientific applications? Do we simply need larger models pretrained on whatever data, be it text, images, or the like? Or do we first need to find the right architecture to scale (as for DeepMind’s GenCeption model)?

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

entry.title: Excavating ground-state human experience
entry.content:
Books Read in July 2026

  1. The Remains of the Day
  2. Extremely Online
  3. Us
  4. How Emotions are Made

Examining the life of a butler

The Remains of the Day, adapted into an Academy Award-winning movie, echoes the fictional contemplations of Stevens, an English butler reflecting on his time serving Lord Darlington, a figure whom Stevens comes to simultaneously revere and question. The book centers on Stevens’ trip away from Darlington Hall, where he served Lord Darlington and Mr. Farraday, the new owner of the estate. On his (rare) journey outside the establishment, Stevens begins to unpack the historical context of his time at Darlington Hall during the Second World War, with nuance and candor. This book offers readers a glimpse into the thought process of a man striving to understand and honor the legacy of an employer with a charming yet checkered reputation.

Setting the digital scene

Curious how we got to today’s sphere of online content creators? What did it take for online video platforms to achieve mass adoption and drive social change along the way? Extremely Online documents the history of this technology’s development, outlining the predecessors of YouTube and TikTok along the trajectory from nascent digital communication to ubiquitous social dialogue. Given how much culture and history is now being shaped by these platforms, it’s worth knowing how they came to prominence.

Vulnerability (or its lack) accumulates

What is a simple word that takes one out of their individualistic context and helps refocus energy on their relationship to others? Us. That is, “us” is a word (and a book by Terrence Real) that restructures how we think about our place in the world. It reminds one that their actions often echo relational patterns carried down generational lines and that these patterns can be reshaped to pave the way for connecting more meaningfully with others. As such, “us” should be used prescriptively to dial down one’s inward focus and dial up one’s capacity for connection.

The atoms of human experience

How Emotions are Made is an instruction manual-and field guide-for how human experience is crafted moment-to-moment. From the neuronal to sociological level, the author Lisa Feldman Barrett carefully walks readers through what makes humans tick, how we make decisions (via emotional cues), the role of emotions in general cognition, and the implications of emotion research showing that emotions are not universally perceived the same way across cultures. All of this carries important caveats for how we can conceptualize our “inner landscapes”, the consequences of these conceptualizations, and how we might view the development of “artificial intelligences” in the wild.

Alex

entry.title: Paving paths between tasks
entry.content:
Bridging the material gaps

A team of researchers from MIT and beyond recently proposed Atomistic Language Models (ALMs) as a new paradigm for generating and understanding properties of 3D (periodic) materials with a single model. The benefit of this approach is that it leverages the large amount of research effort that has been invested in each area of material science independently (e.g., energy and force prediction, crystal structure prediction) to create a unified method mutually beneficial to each area through the magic of backpropagation and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.

ALMs perform well across a range of tasks in material science, including unconditional (or text-guided) crystal generation, structure prediction, and property regression. Luckily for the research community, ALMs are publicly available on HuggingFace, with a new benchmark for text-guided material generation and optimization (ALM-Bench) also available there!

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

Computing the (bio)matrix

Complementary to ALMs is BioMatrix, a comprehensive approach to modeling 3D molecules and proteins. Like ALMs, it relies on bespoke tokenizers for each data domain (i.e., MolStructTok for molecules and GCP-VQVAE for proteins) to equip its base language model (Qwen3) with knowledge of their continuous (geometric) features.

BioMatrix has been benchmarked on 80 prediction or generation tasks involving molecule/protein sequences, structures, or textual descriptions, reaching state-of-the-art for 77/80 tasks. This suggests that multimodality and scaling, as well as pretraining on natural language data, can advance many scientific tasks with minimal task-specific assumptions.

Reflections

Many recent works have pitched a vision of AI for Science models becoming less specialized over time. Do you agree with this vision, or do you think reality will be (a bit) messier and less linear in its simplification trajectory?

Thanks for reading AI4Science! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

entry.title: A look at many industries, individuals, and interests

link.title: A look at many industries, individuals, and interests

entry.content:
Books Read in June 2026

  1. Blood, Sweat, and Pixels
  2. A Mind at Play
  3. Beyond Shame
  4. Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman!
  5. The Bell Jar
  6. Nobody’s Girl
  7. To Gaze Upon Wicked Gods

Behind the (gaming) scenes

Ever wanted to know how video games are made (like, really transformed into those titles you can’t stop playing or thinking about)? Blood, Sweat, and Pixels provides many stories of how iconic video game titles, such as Stardew Valley, came to be what they are today (i.e., a landmark in the industry). Passion surely fuels much of the industry, yet one also has to wonder whether chronic overwork (e.g., unpaid late night and weekend work hours) is simply a function of poor management common in game development firms or instead a necessary evil en route to a creative masterpiece? Time (and therapy) will probably provide a clearer answer as new generations of developers share their stories.

Reconstructing skillful patterns

Sexual shame is a ubiquitous carryover from many cultural traditions. To paraphrase the wise words of Brené Brown, guilt can be adaptive and helpful to promote positive change in one’s life, while shame (especially that which is based on the grounds of ostracization), in practice, is rarely skillful for enacting positive change. Beyond Shame can help one map out the difference between guilt and shame from the perspective of sexual health, in particular for those from certain religious backgrounds. In doing so, it can help you develop a better understanding of yourself and your values, which is almost always an activity with a high return on investment.

Wow, what a quaint lad

Claude Shannon, after whom Anthropic’s Claude model family is named, is known as the father of Information Theory. Many biographies and films of other leading figures in the history of computing, such as Alan Turing, have been published to date, yet Shannon hasn’t received as much attention until the last decade or so. With the publication of A Mind at Play, we now have a biographical window through which to peer into Shannon’s life and upbringing, what made him tick (or more tellingly, what made him curious), and how he viewed the world. My impression after reading this biography is that Shannon, albeit far from a perfect human being (in terms of relationships and sociability), was an exceptionally talented and charming character, resolutely interested in exploring the world through both science and engineering (e.g., through both mathematics and robotics). Another takeaway of mine: we need more Shannons in this world.

Feyman, you’ve done it again!

Like Shannon, Feynman was a curious character who cannot be easily encapsulated in a single description. He played a role in many instrumental discoveries in both science and engineering, and his interests varied widely (like many other historical polymaths). Surely You’re Joking, Mr. Feynman is perhaps the best book to read for a glance into the witty world of Feynman, following him in his travels across America as well as internationally. You probably owe it to yourself to read this book at least once, so you’ll know what all the hubbub of Feynman is about (but don’t just stop there!).

Mental health in a past era

The Bell Jar is a sobering look at the author’s (semi-autobiographical) descent into mental illness in their early 20s, told their various literary devices such as absurdism, psychodelic imagery, and metaphor. The book is firmly rooted in its chosen setting, 1950s America, a time in which mental health (for women, in particular) was often stigmatized and lacked adequate treatment resources. With television adaptations on the horizon, this story is seeing renewed public interest, though it may very well continue to have broad literary impacts in book format.

Trail of trauma

A tale not for the weary of heart, Nobody’s Girl catalogues the journey of Virginia Roberts Giuffre through sex trafficing and, ultimately, through Jeffrey Epstein’s inner circle of human exploitation. Embedded throughout the book are glimpses of Virginia’s psychosocial processing of these events in realtime and how they impacted her life well into adulthood. Many prominent figures’ names appear in the book, while others remain elusive. Currently, it is unclear what impact (if any) the latter (unnamed) figures had on Virginia’s tragic passing not long before this book was published.

History meets fantasy, with the mechanics of magic

To Gaze Upon Wicked Gods offers a satisfying blend of history and fantasy, with the narrative centered in Asia amidst rising geopolitical tensions between an alternative version of Rome and that of the fictional Pangu empire. Taking place during a parody of the Opium Wars in Ancient China, the story focuses on the protagonist, Ruying, and her journey from facing Roman occupation to incidentally ascending the ranks of the same empire. This tale offers a complex, nuanced spin on historically fictional conflicts, with a fantasy (combat) varnish that is hard not to appreciate.

Alex
